ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Services of qualified doctors in the villages 
*521, SHRI KHAGEN DAS: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have conducted a survey to find out 
the number of villages in the country where the services of qualified doctors are 
not available; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps being taken to ensure coverage of all villages by doctors? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) There has been no survey conducted by government to find out the 
number of villages in the country where the services of qualified doctors are not 
available. 
(c) Government is constantly introducing projects and schemes with innumerable 
and innovative interventions in order to expand the outreach and coverage of 
health service delivery in the rural areas. The following steps are being taken 
to improve the availability of 
qualified doctors in the rural areas: 
(1) Since the appointment and postings of doctors is entirely the responsibility 
of the State Governmcnts/UT administrations, the State Govcrnmcnts/UT 
administrations have been advised to take appropriate steps to fill up the 
vacancies' of doctors in rural areas. 
(2) In pursuance of the Resolution of the 6th Conference of Central 
Council of Health and Family Welfare, held in 1999, the States have been 
advised to take the following steps to ensure availability of qualified doctors 
in rural areas. 
 
• To resort to decentralized recruitment of doctors. 
• To appoint of doctors on contractual basis. 
2 

[23 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
• To make rural service obligatory for 3 years, for fresh graduates. 
• To reserve 25% of post-graduate s cats in Medical Colleges, for in 
service candidates who have worked in rural areas for 
3 years. 
(3) Reproductive and Child Health Programme interventions for 
improving the availability of doctors, are: 
• State Government is empowered to appoint anaesthetists and specialists 
on contract basis. 
• 24 hours delivery services has comm enced in some PHC's CHC's with 
honorarium to the staff. 
• There is provision for the contractual hiring of consultant doctors to 
visit PHC's for providing MTP Services at least twice every month. 
• We now have 97 Mother NGOs covering 412 out of 593 districts. 
These MNGOs and their field NGOs su pplement public sector effort at 
advocacy, counselling as well as community level non-clinical services. 
• Practitioners of the Indian Systems of Medicine are being involved in 
the delivery of RCH services. 
(4) Government have adopted the National Population Policy 
2000, which emphasizes the need to augment the existing number 
of trained medical personnel in the rural areas and in other under- 
served segments with diverse health care providers, by: 
• Reviving the earlier system of the licensed medical practitioners. 
• Increasing and augmenting the public-private partnership and providing a 
role for the non-government practioners. 
• Assigning a satellite population to private medical practitioners who may 
be accredited after due certification by the Indian Medical Association 
(IMA). 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [23 April, 2001] 
• Involving the non-medical fraternity in counselling and advocacy. 
• Collaborating with NGOs to augment advocacy, counselling and clinical 
services. 
SHRI KHAGEN DAS: 'Hea lth for All' is the overall aim of the National 
Health Policy which was adopted by the Government of India in 1983, in 
keeping with the Alma Ata Declaration of 1970. Despite some development 
in the health care infrastructure, the health care delivery system in the rural 
areas, where three-fourths of the Indian  population lives, is most inadequate. 
There are urban-rural disparities in health infrastructure. Most of the medical 
services are concentrated in the urban areas. The number of hospital beds per 
lakh population is 20 in the rural areas as compared to 218 in the urban areas. 
There are persistent gaps between the need and the availability of medical 
staff at the primary health centres. Against the national norm of one male and 
female multipurpose health worker per centre which has a population of 
3000—5000, only half the number is sanctioned. There is a shortage of nearly 
one lakh health workers. The number of  pharmacists, lab technicians, X-ray 
technicians, nurses, midwives, etc. is  far short of the requirements. More 
than 10 per cent of the primary health  centres are being run w thout doctors. 
Now, the Minister has stated that the appointment and posting of doctors is 
entirely the responsibility of the State Government. Sir, the Central 
Government formulates the health po licy and the State Government has to 
follow it. In such a situation, the (a) part of my first supplementary is.... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: What was the need to give the background? 
SHRI KHAGEN DAS: This is the back ground, Sir. There is a disparity 
between the rural and the urban areas. 
MR.  CHAIRMAN: My dear friend, the question itself is the background.   
Now   five   minutes   are   lost   in   your   giving   the background. 
SHRI KHAGEN DAS: Sir, the (a) part of my first supplementary is, will 
the Minister tell the House what are th e specific steps the Government has 
taken so far to remove the disparities between the 
4 

[23 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
urban and the rural areas and the inadequacies? Part (b) of my 
supplementary is, is it correct that due to shortage of doctors in different 
parts of the country, particularly, in the tribal, remote, hilly and backward 
areas, the incidence of child mortality and various easily curable diseases is 
very high, compared to the internationally accepted norms? If so, what 
concrete steps and programmes has the Government taken to combat it, 
particularly in the tribal, hilly, remote and backward areas? 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Your background and (a) and (b) parts of the 
supplementary have taken five minutes! 
SHRI A. RAJA: Sir, there are 22,975  Primary Health Centres available 
throughout the country. The total strength sanctioned for the PHCs is 29702. 
The number of existing qualified doctors appointed at present is 25506. Sir, 
353 Primary Health Centres are having four doctors, 947 Primary Health 
Centres are having three doctors and 4585 Primary health Centres aic having 
two doctors. But, it is true that 1463 Primary Health Centres have no doctors 
at all, and as stated in my answer itself, health being a State subject, the State 
Governments have to look after all these things. Inspite of that, as Central 
Government, we are having a Central Council of Health and Family Welfare, 
a statutory body, in this Ministry, and we had convened six meetings of this 
Council. Many suggestions were enumerated during these meetings. The 
important suggestions are as follows. In October 1995, a meeting was 
convened by the Council in which a valuable suggestion was made, that the 
Medical Council of India, which is a statutory body, and which is dealing 
with the prescriptions of doctors, le gislation and other things, should be 
directed to have a fresh look at this thing that the permanent registration for 
doctors should be made only after three years' rural service. Once they have 
completed the M.B.B.S. co urse, all doctors should be compulsorily made 
available for the rural health services, and then only permanent registration 
can be given. This was the first suggestion made in that meeting. While 
responding to the said suggestion, the M.C.I, has stated that is a statutory 
body, that some legal involvements are there to make a disparity between the 
appointments. One thing cannot be given to a particular person. 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [23 April, 2001] 
Apart from that, after a thorough study, the M.C.I, has come forward with a 
study in which is has been stated that there is no inadequacy of doctors in the 
rural areas. It is only the maldistribution of doctors in these areas, which has 
given rise to this problem. The recruitment system, which is being adopted 
invariably by the State governments, st ates as to what the norms for the 
recruitment of doctors are. It does not speak about how doctors should be 
accommodated in rural areas at the time of recruitment. So , the M.C.I., in 
turn, made some recommendations. They recommended that at the time of 
recruitment, the States Governments have to look into the matter of 
appointment of doctors in the rural areas. This recommendation has been 
duly intimated to the States also. We  are getting a response from the State 
Governments.

Statement 
(a) to (c) A comprehensive legislation on Tobacco was introduced by the 
Government in the Rajya Sabha on the 7th March 2001, and covers 
cigarettes as well as other product cont aining tobacco. Cigarettes arc in the 
concurrent list and as such, the Parliament is empowered to legislate on the 
subject of cigarettes. However, as  far as other tobacco products arc 
concerned, these fall within the purview of the State list and as per the 
provisions of Article 252(1) of the Constitution of India, the resolutions from 
the Legislatures of at least two states  arc required if the Parliament is to 
prepare and consider passing of a legislation on the subject.

resolution in their legislatures. A number of other states have expressed their 
support and have given outline of the steps being taken by them against the 
ill effects of tobacco. Further. though it is true that only four states have 
passed resolutions in order to adopt the central legislation on other tobacco 
products at the present time, other stat es can be asked to adopt the law as 
and when it is passed by the Parliament and is enacted.

Statement-II 
National Cancer Control Programme 
There various schemes under National Cancer Control Programme for 
which central assistance is provided to the State Government/Institutions. The 
schemes are as under: 
Development of Oncology Wing 
This scheme is available only for Government Medical Colleges to fill up 
the geographical gaps in the detection and treatment of cancer in the country. 
It has been observed that there is wide geographical gap in the North and 
North-Eastem States. Financial assist ance up to Rs. 2.00 crores can be 
provided to an Institute under the scheme for purchase of listed equipments.   The  
infrastructure  including  staff will   be  provided 
106 

[23 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
by the concerned State Government/Organisation. This is a one time grant. 
Setting up of Cobalt Therapy Unit 
Financial assistance up to Rs. 1.50 cror e is provided to State Government 
for setting up of Cobalt Therapy Unit in Government institutions. Special 
building to house the unit has to be constructed out of their own fund with 
specifications prescribed by BARC, Bombay. The special building should be 
ready before the release of any assist ance for the Cobalt Therapy Unit. This 
is a one-time grant. 
An amount of Rs. 1.00 crore is also provided for Cobalt Therapy Unit to 
the Non-Governmental Organisations on the specific recommendations of 
the State Government. This is a one-time grant. 
Assbtance for Mammography Unit 
The Mammography equipment has also been included under the scheme 
for setting up of Cobalt Therapy Unit. A Central assistance up to Rs. 30.00 
lakhs can be provided to those Institutions/ Organisations who have the 
facilities for treatment of cancer patients and has well-equipped Radiotherapy 
Department. This is also a onetime grant. 
Voluntary Organisation Scheme 
The scheme is for financial assistance up to Rs. 5.00 lakhs to the Voluntary 
Organisations for undertaking health education and early detection activities 
in cancer on the specific recommendations  of the State Government as per 
proforma enclosed. The organisation must  produce proof to the effect that 
they are engaged in cancer control activities for the last 3 years. 
The schemes for Non-Governmental Organisation (NGOs) are governed 
by the provision of GFR 148 to 151. The NGOs should be registered under 
the Societies Registration Act, 1860 and are charitable organizations. As per 
GFR 148, the instituion must have a legal status. As such, the institution 
must be registered under the relevant Act and have a registration certificate. 
It is to be ensured before forwarding their applications to this Ministry for 
grant-in-aid. Further,  the institutions seeking grant-in-aid will be required to 
107 

RAJYA SABHA [23 April, 2001] 
submit an application as per prescribed proforma which should enclose along 
with the Registration Certificate, Artic les of Association, Bye-laws, Audited 
Statement of Accounts, source and pattern of income and expenditure and the 
Annual Reports for the last three years. 
District Cancer Control Programme 
A scheme for district project (duration-five years) for health education, 
detection and pain relief measures under National Cancer Control Programme 
was initiated during the year 1990-91. In this scheme, financial assistance of 
Rs. 15.00 lakh is provided to the State Government/UT administration for 
each district selected un der the scheme with a pr ovision of Rs. 10.00 lakhs 
per annum for each district for the remaining four years of the project period. 
After five year, the project is to be taken over by the State Government. Two 
committees are to be constituted; one at the State level and other at the 
District level. The State Government may issue administrative orders in these 
regards. 
The Utilisation Certificate in respect of the each scheme where grant-in-aid 
was released earlier is required to be submitted. State Government/Institution 
are to ensure that the Utilisation Certificate along with the copies of the 
relevant audited accounts may please be enclosed for ready reference in each 
case.

Print Media Policy 
4023. SHRI NARENDRA M OHAN: Will the Minister of 
INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the print media policy of Government is in accordance with the 
Cabinet Resolution of 13th September, 1955; 
(b) if so, what are the details of this print media policy which is at present in 
existence; 
(c) whether any changes have been incorporated in the print media after the 
Cabinet Resolution of 1955; and 
(d) if so, when and what are these changes? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The existing print media policy, which is guided by the Cabinet decision of 
1955, prohibits publication of foreign owned newspapers/ periodicals in the country 
and the Indian editions of foreign newspapers/periodicals dealing mainly with news 
and current affairs. 
(c) No Sir. 
(d) Does not arise.

Policy for appointment of Judges 
4038. SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHAN DRA REDDY: Will the Minister 
of LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the policy of Government for the appointment of Judges in the Supreme 
Court and High Courts and the guidelines issued in this regard; 
(b) whether it is a fact that posts of Judges are not filled up immediately 
and the vacancies remain vacant for months together; 
(c) if so, whether Government are considering a time-bound programme 
for finalising the names of the Judges a week before vacancy arises; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): (a) to (d) Appointment of Judges of the Supreme 
Court of India and High Courts is made under articles 124 and 217 of the 
Constitution of India respectively. The Memorandum of Procedure regarding 
appointment of Judges, which 
173 

RAJYA SABHA [23 April, 2001] 
has been finalised aftei the Judgement dated 6th October, 1993 of the 
Supreme Court of India read with the Advisory Opinion of 26th October, 
1998, provides that whenever a vacancy is expected to arise in the office of a 
Judge of the Supreme Court, the Chief Justice of India will initiate proposal 
and forward his recommendation to the Union Minister of Law, Justice and 
Company Affairs to fill up the vacancy. 
As regards High Courts, the Memorandum of Procedure provides that 
when a permanent vacancy is expected to  arise in any year in the office of a 
Judge, the Chief Justice of the High Court will as early as possible but at 
least 6 months before the date of occu rrence of the vacancy, communicate to 
the Chief Minister of the State his views on the persons to be selected for 
appointment. The Governor, as advised by the Chief Minister, is expected to 
forward his recommendation as early as possible but not later than 6 weeks 
from the date of receipt of the propos al from the Chief Justice of the High 
Court. 
The Government has recently requested the Chief Justices of the High 
Courts, the Chief Ministers and the Governors of the States to keep the above 
procedure and the time schedule in mind while sending their 
recommendations. 
The vacancies of Judges arise, from  time to time, due to retirement, 
resignation and elevation etc. of the Judges. The filling up vacancies in the 
Supreme Court of India and the High Co urts is a consultative process among 
the constitutional authorities. Every effort is being made to fill up the 
vacancies expeditiously.

Statement 
Gist of main recommendations of the committee on electoral reforms (Dinesh 
Goswami Committee) and their present status: 
1. The Election Commission of India should be a three-member body. 
[Implemented by the Presidential Notification dated 1st October, 1993] 
2. The appointment of Chief Election Commissioner should be in 
consultation with the Chief Justice of India and the Leader of the opposition. 
The Chief Election Commissioner should be consulted for appointment of 
other Members. [The Constitution (Seventieth Amendment) Bill, 1990 
contained a provision regarding appointment of Chief Election 
Commissioner and other Election Commissioners by 
181 

RAJYA SABHA [23 April, 2001] 
the President in consultation with Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, the Speaker 
of the Lok Sabha and the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, which, 
however, lapsed.] 
3. The tenure of the Chief Election Commissioner and other 
Election Commissioner should be for a term of five years or sixty-five 
years of age, whichever is later and they should in no case continue 
in office beyond sixty-five years and for more than ten years in all. 
[The Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners 
(Conditions of Service) Amendment Act, 1993 provides that the tenure 
of the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners 
would be for six years or sixty-five years of age whichever is earlier.] 
4. The Chief Election Commissioner and the Election 
Commissioners should be made ineligible not only for any 
appointment under the Government but also to any office including 
the office of Governor. [The Constitution (Seventieth Amendment) 
Hill, 1990 contained a provision in  this regard, which, however, 
lapsed.) 
5. A fresh delimitation on the basis of 1981 census. Rotation of 
seats reserved for Scheduled Castes. [Two Bills, namely, the 
Constitution (Seventy-first Amendment) Bill, 1990 and the Constitution 
(Eightieth Amendment) Bill, 1996 were introduced in Parliament, 
which were based on the recommendations of the Committee. The 
former, though passed by the Rajy a Sabha and referred to the Lok 
Sabha, was later withdrawn and the latter bill lapsed on dissolution of 
the House (Lok Sabha). The Government has again introduced the 
Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Bill, 2000 in the Lok Sabha on 
27.11.2000 which seeks to extend the existing constitutional embargo 
on undertaking readjustment of electoral constituencies upto the year 
2026 as also to undertake readjustment and rationalization of the 
constituencies, including those reserved for the Scheduled Castes and 
the Scheduled Tribes, based on the population census for the year 
1991, without altering the number of seats allocated to States in the 
Lok Sabha and State Legislative Asse mblies. So far as the issue of 
rotation of reserved constituencies is concerned, the Constitution 
(Seventy-first Amendment) Bill, 1990 contained a provision in this 
182 

[23  April, 2001] RAJYA  SABHA 
regard but the Select Committee of Parliament, which considered the Bill, 
was of the view that there was no n eed for such a specific provision as 
Parliament under article 327 was competent to enact a law for rotation of 
seats. The present Bill also does not contain a provision in this regard in 
view of lack of political consensus, which was reflected in the meeting of 
political parties held on 13.5.2000 to consider the issue of fresh delimitation 
of constituencies and other allied issues.] 
6. Introduction of multi-purpose photo identity cards. [The scheme of 
issuance of photo identity cards to voters has been accepted by Government. 
Multi-purpose use of these cards has been allowed. The Election 
Commission is in overall charge of the scheme. So far, 63.48% of electors all 
over the country have been issued these Cards.] 
7. No individual to be allowed to contest from more than two 
constituencies. [Implemented by the Representation of the People 
(Amendment) Act, 1996] 
8. Non-serious candidates to be discouraged. Security deposit of 
independent candidates to be raised. [Implemented by the Representation of 
the People (Amendment) Act, 1996] 
9. Forfeiture of security deposit for failure to secure less than l/4th of the 
votes polled. [The Representation of the People (Second Amendment) Bill, 
1994 contained a provision in this regard, which, however, lapsed.] 
 
10. Statutory backing for important provisions of model code of conduct.

† 4054. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of SOCIAL 
JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 50 per cent burden in cottage and small industries 
like animal husbandry, agriculture, forestry, popultry farming, food processing 
etc. is shouldered by women and these womenfolks remain "invisible workers"; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that these women do not get even the 
minimum wages nor any pay scales matching with that of their male 
counterparts; and 
(c) if so, the steps being taken by Government to provide these women with 
the wages equivalent to their male counterparts? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI): (a) to (c) As 
per the information provided by the Ministry of Labour who are dealing with the 
subject, women workers in the concerned sectors come under the unorganized 
sector and their wages are paid as per provisions of the Minimum Wages Act, 
1948. The Act does not make any distinction on the basis of sex. The Equal 
Remuneration Act, 1976 which extends to the whole of India, provides for 
equal remuneration to women for the same work or work of a similar nature. The 
Central Government is the appropriate Government in relation to any employment 
carried on by or under the authority of the Central Government or railway 
administration, or in relation to a banking company, a mine, oilfield or major port 
of any corporation established by or under a Central Government Act. In respect of 
all other employments, the State Government are the appropriate governments. 
Under the Act, Officers of the appropriate government notified as Inspectors make 
inspections and prosecute those found violating provisions of the Act. The Central 
Government monitors implementation of the Act. Considering the special 
problems of the women workers and in order to pre-empt their

damage or major cracks were noticed and also no complaints from any 
Municipal Departments and private builder regarding damage of property

the pillar wall separating the lobby area of the 5th

(a) whether Government are aware of th e large scale evasion of property 
tax on account of under statement of the value of the property; and

concerned, no information is availabl e about large scale evasion of property

4092. SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI:  
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
Will the Minister of URBA N DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Mega-City Scheme is presently under 
implementation; 
(b) if so, the cities that are covered under the scheme; 
(c) the criteria for selection of the cities and whether any city from 
Rajasthan has been selected; and 
(d) the objectives of the scheme and the progress made under the scheme, 
so far? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) to (d) A Centrally Sponsored Scheme called "Mega 
City Scheme" was initiated in 1993-94 with the objective of developing city 
wide Infrastructure with inbuilt cost recovery measures to create a Revolving 
Fund, with a view to enable the cities to tackle the problems due to migration 
from rural areas over which city authorities have no control. The projects 
taken up under the Scheme relate to urban infrastructure, including water 
supply, sewerage, drainage, sanitation, city transport, land development, slum 
improvement, solid waste management, construction of roads, urban renewal 
etc. 
The cities of Mumbai, Kolkata, Che nnai, Hyderabad and Bangalore were 
selected on the criteria of having population of 40 lakhs and above as per 
1991 Census. No city from Rajasthan qualified on the basis of population 
criteria. 
In all 394 projects costing Rs. 3377.70 crores have been approved upto 
31.12.2000, out of which 128 have been completed and 266 projects are 
under implementation or are to be taken up for implementation.

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Recent incidents on Indo-Bangladesh Border 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNA L AFFAIRS AND MINISTER 
OF DEFENCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): Hon. Members are aware of 
the grave incidents on the India-Bangladesh border during 16 th-19th 
April, 2001, caused by the unwar ranted and unprovoked intrusion by 
BDR forces into the village of Pyriduwah, in the East Khasi Hill District 
of Meghalaya.

version of the Debate.

[23 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
Tension thereafter spread to other sectors, including in Assam 
where there was heavy exchange of fire between BSF and BDR in 
Boratbari on the night of April 17-18. On is ,h April morning, one of the 
BSF patrol parties went missing. Ther eafter, we learnt with concern 
that Bangladesh media had reported  a statement by the Director 
General, BDR, that 16 BSF per sonnel had been killed in an 
encounter. 
The matter was immediately taken up through the regular 
channels of the BSF as also through diplomatic channels both in Delhi 
and in Dhaka, to convey our grav e concern at this unprovoked and 
unwarranted intrusion by BDR and ca lling for immediate cessation of 
firing, withdrawal of BD R and restoration of the status quo ante. 
Confirmation was received from the Bangladesh Government, the 
same night (ia m April), that necessary instructions were being issued 
for withdrawal of the BDR and restoration of status QUO ante. This 
withdrawal was completed by the night of 19th April. 
When the bodies of our BSF personnel were returned on 20"' 
evening, as demanded by us, shocking marks of injury and mutilation, 
as also evidence of 8 of them having been shot at point blank range 
were found. In the case of Deputy Commandant Mandal, rigor-mortis 
was just setting in, indicating that death had occurred within the last 
24 hours. The marks of injury on all bodies were recorded and signed 
by representatives of both BSF and BDR. 
A strong protest was lodged with the Government of 
Bangladesh at the inhuman treatment of our BSF personnel. We have 
been assured by the Bangladesh Gove rnment that all aspects of 
these incidents would be investigat ed, also that the BDR action was 
taken without their knowledge and wa s regrettable. Prime Minister 
Sheikh Hasina has spoken to Prime Minister Vajpayee last night. The 
Prime Minister conveyed to her India's deep sense of hurt and 
anguish over the inhuman treatment meted out to our BSF personnel. 
Sheikh Hasina stated that she,  too, was deeply saddened and 
concerned by these incidents and confirmed that a full investigation 
would be carried out into all aspects of the incidents, including the 
mutilation of the bodies of the BSF personnel. 
Earlier, I had received a call from the Bangladesh Foreign 
Minister, expressing exactly the same sentiment, 
I would like to reiterate that st rong ties of friendship exist 
between the two countries, and acts of criminal adventurism should 
not be permitted

to affect these ties, It is now upto the Government of Bangladesh to 
act against the perpetrators of these crimes and restore confidence and 
trust.

admiration for the selfless sacrific e of our brave BSF personnel, Our

THE LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION (DR. MANMOHAN 
SINGH}: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the totally unwarranted and unprovoked 
intrusion by the BDR forces into the Indian territories, and the ghastly 
and brutal killings of brave jawans of the BSF, have sent shock waves 
in our country. All sections of public opinion in this country have nothing 
but condemnation for what has been done, more so, because 
Bangladesh happens to be a friendly neighbour. We have close and 
cordial ties with that country, that this incident should have taken place 
on the borders of two friendly countries, is all the more a saddening 
affair. Mr. Chairman, Sir, it goes without saying that there must be a 
completely impartial inquiry into this whole incident. The way our brave 
jawans have been treated, the inhuman treatment that has been meted 
out to them, in total violation of all norms of civiliz ed behaviour, is 
something, we as a nation, cannot accept, and the least that should be 
done, is an impartial inquiry, with which I do believe, our people should 
be associated, to find out how such ghastly crimes have been

responsible for these ghastly crimes, will, in fact, be brought to book. Sir,

hope I am wrong. But there are worries about the intelligence failure

SHRI JIBON ROY (West Bengal): I condemn the killing of the 
Border Security Force personnel. I join in the anguish expressed 
inside the House, by hon. Members,  as well as by people outside the 
House, against the ghastly murder. I condole the deaths. I do not wish 
to be too much critical or make critical references against the 
Government at this critical moment of time. At the same time, I must 
say that it is a shame that we came to know about the killing of our 
jawans and their being taken away, from a foreign radio. There was no 
information either with the Home Ministry or with the Armed Forces. 
This reflects the callous situation of this Government and the absence 
of political sagacity too. 
All the more, I do not think thai a solution lies only in military 
action, as far as this border clash is concerned. It is, simply, not a 
border clash. It implies something more. There is a deliberate attempt. 
Both the countries are friendly countries. We have improved our 
relations with the Government of Bangladesh, I am glad that the 
Bangladesh premier has at least said that she was saddened and that 
she has not recognised the action taken on the border. But it is clear 
that there is a deliberate attempt to strain the relations between the 
two countries in the sub-contin ent. After the statement of the 
Bangladesh Prime Minister, it is clear that there is a deliberate attempt 
to strain the relations. 
Secondly, it should be kept in mind that, on our side, two 
border States are going to the elections. Bangladesh is also going to 
the elections. The present Government of Bangladesh, led by Sheikh 
Hasina, is consistently fighting t he religious fundamentalism in that 
country. All the fundamentalist forces are ganging up there. In such a 
situation, there may be another motive, besides creating a strained 
relation between the two countries, to foment communal tension along 
our borders, in Assam and West Bengal. Therefore, a multi-
dimensional target was there in this act. 
Hence, I. would suggest that we should not make any 
passionate statement. We should view it in depth. We should see that, 
in any case, our relations with Bangladesh are not strained, I caution 
about that, because if we lose Bangladesh as our friendly neighbour, 
we lose almost the entire subcontinent. Of course, the military 
preparedness has to be there. No friendship works unless you are 
powerful. 
There were only 14 or 15 Border Security Force personnel 
from our side, whereas a thousand forces were there on the other 
side, It implies a 
305 

RAJYA SABHA [23 April, 2001]  
weakness on our part. Therefore, there should be military 
preparedness always. The entire border with Bangladesh-along West 
Bengal, Assam and Meghalaya-- has to be protected at any cost. The 
military arrangements have to be made . At the same time, a cautious 
political approach should be there, bec ause, basically, it is a political 
and diplomatic solution that helps in strengthening the relations. 
Diplomatic and political sagacity is required. That has to be 
maintained. In no case the relations between the peoples of the two 
countries should be allowed to be strained. The previous United Front 
Government had taken initiatives in resolving the water dispute. It 
brought Bangladesh closer to India. Such attempts have to be made. 
There. religious fundamentalism and IS I activities are trying to strain 
the relations with India. 
So. I urge upon the Government to view it comprehensively 
and take appropriate step, including military steps. With these words, I 
conclude. 
Thank you.

SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN {Karnataka): Madam Deputy 
Chairman. the statement made by t he hon. Defence Minister and the 
Foreign Minister on the recent incidents on the Indo-Bangladesh 
border is unfortunate. The statemen t does not contain facts and it

to come before the Parliament to say that 16 of its jawans were killed 
and murdered in cold-blood. There are so many questions that we 
have to ask and the Government ha s to answer those questions and 
provide information to the House. The House is unanimous in saying 
that there has been an Intelligence failure. Nobody, including the ruling

there was no Intelligence failure and that the Bangladesh Government
